title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) loop for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 stratified intent→configuration tasks) we compared (1) baseline — a single shared LLM proposal per task, and (2) guarded — the identical shared proposal validated by a deterministic verifier and allowed at most one automated repair iteration when the verifier flagged preregistered high/medium-severity violations. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002; paired-bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). The archived exact McNemar two-sided test was implemented as an exact binomial on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01) per the executor convention; observed two-sided p = 1.00. Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and the tested model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; the marginal pass-rate gain for a single-repair guarded budget is therefore small, though the verifier converted one concrete baseline failure into a verified pass. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly used for intent-driven NetOps tasks: translating operator intent into device configuration, multi-step change plans, and limited automated repair. Prior systems and surveys emphasize that operational safety depends on surrounding engineering (deterministic validators, sandboxes, canarying, rollback) rather than the model alone [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. The generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) architecture—candidate generation by an LLM, deterministic verification of formalized properties, and automated or human-assisted repair—is widely advocated but quantitatively under-studied in controlled ablation settings that isolate the verifier’s marginal contribution. Practically, operators must know: when an LLM already produces high-quality candidates, how much incremental safety does a verifier plus a modest automated-repair budget provide on an operative pass/fail metric? We answer this precisely with a preregistered paired experiment that holds the LLM proposal fixed (shared-initial_candidate semantics) and measures verifier+single-repair impact on a deterministic verifier-scoped pass/fail outcome.
sections.related_work: Deterministic verification methods for network configurations (header-space analysis, Batfish-style analyzers, route-model verifiers) enable machine-checkable properties such as reachability, isolation, and update atomicity and form the technical foundation for verifier-in-the-loop NetOps engineering [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent NetOps/AIOps and intent-translation systems integrate LLMs while recommending guardrails and verifier-assisted workflows (INTA, Confucius, and related agentic frameworks) but rarely report controlled ablations isolating verifier impact [INTA, 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–validate–repair patterns also appear across structured-generation domains as a mitigation for incorrect or unsafe model outputs [PoeTone; PropertyGPT]. Separately, failure-mode studies of LLM agents motivate verification and human oversight to address hallucination, overconfidence, and tool-integration errors [Owen, 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2025]. Our contribution is an artifact-backed, preregistered paired measurement that isolates verifier+repair effect under canonical, deterministic semantics.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. We preregistered study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026 and froze the research question, strata, seeds, estimands, analysis executor, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rule prior to observing outcomes. Primary confirmatory hypothesis: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration will produce a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback (paired within-task). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations.

Task generation and strata. A deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks was generated with deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 using preregistered seeds and stratified into three clusters per the preregistered sampling_plan: VLAN-change = 167 tasks, ACL-change = 167 tasks, static-route-change = 166 tasks. No confirmatory exclusions occurred; the realized per-cluster counts match the preregistered allocation (167/167/166) and are recorded in the archived task_manifest.jsonl (execution artifact). The generator constrained allowed features to {admin, mtu, vlan} to align with the deterministic verifier’s modeled scope; the full manifest with required_sequence and expected_final_state is archived.

Generation semantics, models, and verifier. To isolate verifier effect we used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" (independent_condition_generation = false): each task produced a single shared LLM proposal that served both as the baseline output and as the input to the guarded arm. Requested LLM = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses) called via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; execution/model_configuration.json records parameters (max_output_tokens = 2000, single-attempt generation). The deterministic verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5; validator specification and violation-code→severity mapping are archived. The guarded arm invoked up to one automated repair iteration only if that verifier reported a preregistered high/medium-severity violation on the shared candidate.

Statistical test and exact implementation. The preregistered confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two-sided test on paired binary outcomes. The archived analysis executor implements the exact two-sided McNemar as an exact binomial on the discordant pair count n = n10 + n01 with observed count k = n10 (the number of pairs where guarded passes and baseline fails under the executor’s discordant-ordering convention). The two-sided p-value used in the archived executor is computed as p_two-sided = 2 × min{P[X ≤ k], P[X ≥ k]} for X ∼ Binomial(n, 0.5), truncated at 1.0; this implementation, source code path, and rationale are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CIs for the absolute paired-success difference were computed with B = 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), resampling pairs with replacement while preserving pairing.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes. The run completed with complete_pair_count = 500 and model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair-stage calls observed = 1). Aggregated per-condition counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). Paired contingency (guarded × baseline): n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002. Paired-bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729).

Exact McNemar implementation and p-value. Applying the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention (n = n10 + n01 = 1, k = n10 = 1) yields the archived two-sided p = 1.00 under the executor’s doubling/truncation rule described above. Small n produces non-intuitive exact p-values; p = 1.00 here indicates the observed discordant pattern is not unusual under the null when only one discordant pair exists. The analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json; analysis_log.jsonl) include the exact code-path and RNG seeds used.

Discordant episode provenance. The single observed repair-stage call generated the sole discordant pair (n10 = 1): the guarded arm converted one baseline-detected violation into a verified pass. The execution manifests and raw-results archive record exactly one such episode. The discordant pair is deterministically locatable in the archived execution/raw_results.jsonl by filtering for entries where baseline scoring indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) and guarded scoring indicates pass == 1; deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms exactly one matching pair exists. The full validator diagnostics, normalized configurations, and repair-provider traces for that pair are archived and preserved under execution/* for deterministic inspection (we do not reproduce provider traces inline here). Representative per-task exemplars (execution/scoring/task-00000X-*.json) are included in the evidence bundle; the repaired episode’s provider-call accounting is consistent with model_calls_used = 501 and repair-stage calls = 1.

Secondary analyses and power considerations. The preregistration's power calculation assumed baseline error prevalence ≈ 0.30 to detect a 10-point absolute reduction with N ≈ 384. Observed baseline failure prevalence (1/500) produced a ceiling effect that reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements on the composite pass metric; consequently, per-violation-class secondary analyses are uninformative because counts are near zero. Missingness and contamination diagnostics report zero confirmatory exclusions and failed episodes (analysis/missingness_summary.csv, contamination_summary.csv).
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation. Under the constrained experimental regime—single requested model (gpt-5-mini), shared_initial_candidate semantics, verifier coverage limited to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}, and at most one automated repair—the LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals and the marginal measured pass-rate benefit of adding the verifier was small (0.002). This conditional result documents a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal quality is very high on verifier-modeled properties, modest verifier+repair budgets may yield negligible measurable pass-rate gains on a composite binary metric, despite correcting rare concrete failures.

Design-choice implications. The shared-initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolate verifier+repair effect conditional on identical proposals; this answers the operational question of marginal verifier utility when regeneration costs are constrained or when policy requires repairing a single human-reviewed proposal. Alternative operational choices—verifier-guided regeneration, larger repair budgets, or cost-weighted objectives—are outside this preregistered design and may yield different effect sizes.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration, deterministic seeds, and automated replacement rules; no manual adjudication occurred. Construct validity: the pass==no high/medium-severity-violation outcome is defined relative to the verifier’s modeled feature set and severity mapping (archived validator-spec); properties outside that coverage are not assessed and would alter operational conclusions. External validity: single-model testing (gpt-5-mini requested), synthetic deterministic corpus, and a single validator limit claims about cross-vendor, cross-model, or production generality. Conclusion validity: observed baseline failure prevalence was far lower than assumed in the power plan, producing the ceiling-effect and limiting sensitivity to detect modest improvements. All such limitations are documented and supported by archived artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) that isolated the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), yielding an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the executor’s exact-binomial convention). This conditional measurement emphasizes a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal quality is high for verifier-modeled properties and verifier coverage is limited, modest verifier+repair budgets may produce negligible measured pass-rate gains on a composite metric, though verifiers can still correct rare concrete failures. We recommend practitioners measure baseline verifier-scoped error prevalence on representative workloads, align verifier coverage with operator-critical properties, and select generation/repair semantics that match deployment priorities. All preregistration, code, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call logs, and analysis artifacts are archived for deterministic re-inspection.

limitations: Synthetic deterministic corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; tasks constrained to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single requested model family (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); no claim of multi-model or cross-validator generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the archived exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the small discordant count.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl in the evidence bundle. To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for entries where baseline scoring indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) and guarded scoring indicates pass == 1; because exactly one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this lookup returns the single episode and its provider-call traces. The validator violation-code→severity mapping is archived in the execution manifest and validator-spec artifacts.
